claim: Malaria caused over 200 million new infections in 2017
source: Malaria is still a major global health threat with over 200 million new infections and around 400,000 deaths in 2017 (World Health Organization, 2018).
evidence: Cited from World Health Organization, 2018 publication

claim: Malaria caused around 400,000 deaths in 2017
source: Malaria is still a major global health threat with over 200 million new infections and around 400,000 deaths in 2017 (World Health Organization, 2018).
evidence: Cited from World Health Organization, 2018 publication

claim: Anemia is a common complication associated with malaria
source: Anemia is a common complication associated with malaria that contributes significantly to the great morbidity and mortality associated with the disease (White, 2018).

claim: Anemia contributes significantly to morbidity and mortality in malaria
source: Anemia is a common complication associated with malaria that contributes significantly to the great morbidity and mortality associated with the disease (White, 2018).

claim: Malaria causes clearance of both infected and uninfected erythrocytes
source: The difficulty in studying this syndrome arises at least in part from its multi-factorial etiology, as malaria causes both the clearance (through complement-mediated lysis or phagocytosis) of infected and uninfected erythrocytes and bone marrow dyserythropoiesis (Lamikanra et al., 2007; White, 2018).
evidence: Cited from Lamikanra et al., 2007 and White, 2018

claim: Malaria causes bone marrow dyserythropoiesis
source: The difficulty in studying this syndrome arises at least in part from its multi-factorial etiology, as malaria causes both the clearance (through complement-mediated lysis or phagocytosis) of infected and uninfected erythrocytes and bone marrow dyserythropoiesis (Lamikanra et al., 2007; White, 2018).
evidence: Cited from Lamikanra et al., 2007 and White, 2018

claim: For each erythrocyte lysed directly due to Plasmodium falciparum infection, about eight uninfected erythrocytes are killed
source: The clearance of uninfected erythrocytes is thought to contribute significantly to anemia, because for each erythrocyte lysed directly due to Plasmodium infection, about eight uninfected erythrocytes are killed in P. falciparum infections (Jakeman et al., 1999; Price et al., 2001)
evidence: Cited from Jakeman et al., 1999 and Price et al., 2001

claim: For each erythrocyte lysed directly due to Plasmodium vivax infection, about 34 uninfected erythrocytes are killed
source: about 34 erythrocytes are killed in P. vivax infections (Collins et al., 2003).

claim: The anti-parasite B-cell antibody response during malaria blood stage is an essential component of protective immunity
source: The anti-parasite B-cell antibody response that is generated during the malaria blood stage represents an essential component of the protective immune response against this disease (Doolan et al., 2009; Portugal et al., 2013).
evidence: Cited from Doolan et al., 2009 and Portugal et al., 2013

claim: Autoantibodies mediate some malaria-associated pathologies
source: However, an important autoimmune response is also generated during malaria, in which autoantibodies mediate some of the associated pathologies (Hart et al., 2016; Rivera-Correa and Rodriguez, 2018; Rivera-Correa, 2016).
evidence: Cited from Hart et al., 2016; Rivera-Correa and Rodriguez, 2018; Rivera-Correa, 2016

claim: Autoantibodies targeting membrane phosphatidylserine on uninfected erythrocytes promote anemia during malaria in mouse models
source: Specifically, autoantibodies that target membrane phosphatidylserine (PS) on uninfected erythrocytes promote anemia during malaria in mouse models, and these autoantibodies correlate with low hemoglobin levels in a cohort of P.-falciparum- and P.-vivax-infected patients with malarial anemia (Barber et al., 2019; Fernandez-Arias et al., 2016)
evidence: Cited from Barber et al., 2019 and Fernandez-Arias et al., 2016

claim: Anti-phosphatidylserine autoantibodies correlate with low hemoglobin levels in P. falciparum and P. vivax infected patients with malarial anemia
source: Specifically, autoantibodies that target membrane phosphatidylserine (PS) on uninfected erythrocytes promote anemia during malaria in mouse models, and these autoantibodies correlate with low hemoglobin levels in a cohort of P.-falciparum- and P.-vivax-infected patients with malarial anemia (Barber et al., 2019; Fernandez-Arias et al., 2016)
evidence: Cited from Barber et al., 2019 and Fernandez-Arias et al., 2016

claim: B-cells expressing transcription factor T-bet secrete autoantibodies in different autoimmune mouse models
source: An atypical group of B-cells that express the transcription factor T-bet secrete autoantibodies in different autoimmune mouse models (Rubtsova et al., 2015; Rubtsova et al., 2017)
evidence: Cited from Rubtsova et al., 2015 and Rubtsova et al., 2017

claim: T-bet+ B-cells are major producers of anti-PS antibodies in mouse malaria
source: An atypical group of B-cells that express the transcription factor T-bet secrete autoantibodies in different autoimmune mouse models (Rubtsova et al., 2015; Rubtsova et al., 2017) and were found to be major producers of anti-PS antibodies in mouse malaria (Rivera-Correa et al., 2017).

claim: T-bet+ B-cells have been identified in the circulation of individuals from malaria-endemic areas
source: B-cells expressing the transcription factor T-bet have been identified in the circulation of individuals from malaria-endemic areas and implicated in the memory response against Plasmodium (Guthmiller et al., 2017)

claim: T-bet+ B-cells are considered atypical memory B-cells
source: B-cells expressing the transcription factor T-bet have been identified in the circulation of individuals from malaria-endemic areas and implicated in the memory response against Plasmodium (Guthmiller et al., 2017), being considered atypical memory B-cells (Obeng-Adjei et al., 2017; Weiss et al., 2009).
evidence: Cited from Obeng-Adjei et al., 2017 and Weiss et al., 2009

claim: Atypical memory B-cells secrete low levels of antibodies
source: These cells are characterized as secreting low levels of antibodies and by inhibitory phenotypic markers such as FcRL5 (Sullivan et al., 2015).

claim: Atypical memory B-cells are characterized by inhibitory phenotypic markers such as FcRL5
source: These cells are characterized as secreting low levels of antibodies and by inhibitory phenotypic markers such as FcRL5 (Sullivan et al., 2015).

claim: The cohort of P. falciparum-infected returned travelers from Germany suffered from mild anemia with average hemoglobin levels of 12.4 g/dL (males) and 10.2 g/dL (females)
source: This cohort suffered from mild anemia with average hemoglobin levels of 12.4 g/dL (males) and 10.2 g/dL (females) (normal range is 13.8 to 17.2 and 12.1 to 15.1 g/dL, respectively) (Table 1).
evidence: Data from patient cohort presented in Table 1

claim: Normal hemoglobin range is 13.8 to 17.2 g/dL for males and 12.1 to 15.1 g/dL for females
source: This cohort suffered from mild anemia with average hemoglobin levels of 12.4 g/dL (males) and 10.2 g/dL (females) (normal range is 13.8 to 17.2 and 12.1 to 15.1 g/dL, respectively) (Table 1).

claim: Hemoglobin levels do not significantly correlate with parasitemia in the cohort of P. falciparum-infected returned travelers
source: As described before in other cohorts with mild anemia (Fernandes et al., 2008; Sumbele et al., 2016), hemoglobin levels in this cohort do not significantly correlate with parasitemia (Figure 1A)
evidence: Data shown in Figure 1A and cited from Fernandes et al., 2008 and Sumbele et al., 2016

claim: Direct erythrocyte infection by Plasmodium is not a major cause of anemia
source: hemoglobin levels in this cohort do not significantly correlate with parasitemia (Figure 1A), confirming that direct erythrocyte infection by Plasmodium is not a major cause of anemia
evidence: Inference from lack of correlation shown in Figure 1A

claim: Anti-PS IgG antibodies inversely correlate with hemoglobin levels in P. falciparum-infected returned travelers
source: We observed an inverse correlation between anti-PS antibodies and hemoglobin levels (Figure 1B)

claim: Anti-PfEBA IgG antibodies do not correlate with hemoglobin levels in P. falciparum-infected returned travelers
source: We observed an inverse correlation between anti-PS antibodies and hemoglobin levels (Figure 1B), which was not found for IgG antibodies against the P. falciparum erythrocyte binding antigen (PfEBA) (Figure 1C)

claim: Plasma anti-erythrocyte IgG antibodies correlate with the development of malarial anemia in P. falciparum-infected returned travelers
source: our results show that plasma anti-erythrocyte IgG antibodies also correlate with the development of malarial anemia, showing a significant negative correlation with hemoglobin from the samples of P.-falciparum-infected returned travelers (Figure 1D).

claim: Anti-erythrocyte antibodies recognize all kinds of antigens in human erythrocyte lysates, including PS
source: These antibodies recognized all kinds of antigens in human erythrocyte lysates (Mourão et al., 2018; Mourão et al., 2016), including PS.
evidence: Cited from Mourão et al., 2018 and Mourão et al., 2016

claim: Anti-DNA IgG antibodies do not correlate with anemia in P. falciparum-infected returned travelers
source: our results show that anti-DNA IgG antibodies, which are typical in autoimmune diseases (Tsokos, 2011), do not correlate with anemia (Figure 1E)
evidence: Data shown in Figure 1E and cited from Tsokos, 2011

claim: Anti-DNA antibodies are typical in autoimmune diseases
source: our results show that anti-DNA IgG antibodies, which are typical in autoimmune diseases (Tsokos, 2011)

claim: Malarial anemia is characterized by the lysis of uninfected erythrocytes
source: As malarial anemia is characterized by the lysis of uninfected erythrocytes and by an increase in lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) in the plasma (Fendel et al., 2010)

claim: Malarial anemia is characterized by an increase in lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) in the plasma
source: As malarial anemia is characterized by the lysis of uninfected erythrocytes and by an increase in lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) in the plasma (Fendel et al., 2010)

claim: Anti-PS IgG antibodies positively correlate with LDH levels in P. falciparum patient plasma
source: we determined whether anti-PS IgG antibodies correlate with the levels of LDH in the patient's plasma (Figure 2A). We observed a significant positive correlation

claim: Plasma from P. falciparum-infected patients is significantly more effective than healthy control plasma in lysing human erythrocytes exposing PS
source: Using an in vitro complement lysis assay of human erythrocytes exposing PS, we observed that plasma from patients was significantly more effective than healthy control plasma in lysing human erythrocytes (Figure 2B).

claim: Anti-PS IgG antibody levels directly correlate with erythrocyte lysis capacity in P. falciparum patient plasma
source: We then studied the relation of anti-PS IgG levels and the erythrocyte lysis capacity in the patient's plasma, as determined using the in vitro complement lysis assay. We observed a direct correlation between anti-PS and erythrocyte lysis capacity (Figure 2C)

claim: Pre-incubation of erythrocytes with annexin V partially reduces erythrocyte lysis capacity in P. falciparum patient plasma samples
source: To determine the anti-PS specificity of the erythrocyte lysis, we pre-incubated the erythrocytes with annexin V, a protein that specifically binds to PS and inhibits the binding of anti-PS antibodies (Fernandez-Arias et al., 2016; van Engeland et al., 1998), finding a partial reduction of the erythrocyte lysis capacity in the plasma samples (Figure 2D).
evidence: Data shown in Figure 2D and cited from Fernandez-Arias et al., 2016 and van Engeland et al., 1998

claim: Annexin V specifically binds to PS and inhibits the binding of anti-PS antibodies
source: we pre-incubated the erythrocytes with annexin V, a protein that specifically binds to PS and inhibits the binding of anti-PS antibodies (Fernandez-Arias et al., 2016; van Engeland et al., 1998)
evidence: Cited from Fernandez-Arias et al., 2016 and van Engeland et al., 1998

claim: FcRL5+T-bet+ B-cells are expanded in PBMC samples from P. falciparum-infected German returned travelers compared to uninfected German controls
source: After gating out non-B-cells (CD19–), we observed that FcRL5+T-bet+ B-cells are indeed expanded in the PBMC samples from P.-falciparum-infected German returned travelers when compared to samples from uninfected German controls (Figure 3B).

claim: There is no significant difference in the levels of atypical MBCs between tourists and VFR groups in P. falciparum-infected returned travelers
source: We did not observe any significant difference in the levels of atypical MBCs in the PBMC between these two groups (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).

claim: There is no significant gender difference in the levels of FcRL5+T-bet+ B-cells in PBMC from P. falciparum-infected patients
source: We also observed no significant gender difference between the levels of FcRL5+T-bet+ B-cells in PBMC (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).

claim: There is no significant correlation between time after treatment and hemoglobin levels in P. falciparum-infected patients
source: Furthermore, we found no significant correlation between the time after treatment at which samples were obtained (ranging from 0 to 31 days, Table 1) and the level of hemoglobin
evidence: Data from patient cohort in Table 1

claim: There is a significant direct correlation between the levels of atypical MBCs and days after treatment in P. falciparum-infected patients
source: We also observed a significant direct correlation between the levels of atypical MBCs and the days after treatment, which suggests that the levels of these cells continue to increase after treatment.

claim: Atypical MBCs inversely correlate with hemoglobin levels in P. falciparum patients
source: We found a significant inverse correlation between hemoglobin levels and atypical MBCs levels in the PBMC samples from P. falciparum patients (Figure 4A).

claim: Atypical MBCs do not significantly correlate with parasitemia in P. falciparum patients
source: Atypical MBCs did not significantly correlate with other relevant parameters such as parasitemia (Figure 4—figure supplement 3)

claim: Atypical MBCs positively correlate with the age of P. falciparum patients
source: Atypical MBCs did not significantly correlate with other relevant parameters such as parasitemia (Figure 4—figure supplement 3), but did correlate positively with the age of the patient (Figure 4—figure supplement 4)

claim: There is no significant correlation between atypical MBCs and thrombocyte counts in P. falciparum patients
source: We did not observe any significant correlation between the levels of atypical MBCs and thrombocyte counts in our cohort of patients (Figure 4—figure supplement 5)

claim: Classical memory B-cells have a significant positive correlation with hemoglobin levels in P. falciparum patients
source: Interestingly, we observed that classical memory B-cells (CD27+CD21+) had a significant positive correlation with hemoglobin levels (Figure 4B).

claim: Plasma cells have a significant positive correlation with hemoglobin levels in P. falciparum patients
source: We did not find any significant correlation between hemoglobin level and percentage of naïve B-cells or immature B-cells, but observed a significant positive correlation with percentage of plasma cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 6).

claim: FcRL5+T-bet+ atypical MBCs positively correlate with anti-PS IgG antibodies in P. falciparum-infected patients
source: Our results show a significant positive correlation between FcRL5+T-bet+ atypical MBCs and anti-PS IgG antibodies (Figure 5A)

claim: Classical MBCs inversely correlate with anti-PS IgG antibodies in P. falciparum-infected patients
source: In accordance with the hemoglobin results (Figure 4B), we also found a significant inverse relationship between anti-PS IgG antibodies and classical MBCs (CD27+CD21+) (Figure 5B).

claim: Naïve B-cells do not significantly correlate with anti-PS IgG antibody levels in P. falciparum patients
source: As shown before for hemoglobin (Figure 4—figure supplement 6), neither naïve nor immature B-cells presented a significant correlation with the levels of plasma anti-PS IgG antibodies (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).

claim: Immature B-cells do not significantly correlate with anti-PS IgG antibody levels in P. falciparum patients
source: As shown before for hemoglobin (Figure 4—figure supplement 6), neither naïve nor immature B-cells presented a significant correlation with the levels of plasma anti-PS IgG antibodies (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).

claim: Plasma cells do not correlate with anti-PS IgG antibodies in P. falciparum patients
source: Plasma cells, which previously correlated with hemoglobin levels, did not correlate with anti-PS IgG antibodies

claim: There is a significant negative correlation between the levels of classical and FcRL5+T-bet+ atypical MBCs in P. falciparum patients
source: Accordingly, we found a significant negative correlation between the levels of classical and FcRL5+T-bet+ atypical MBCs (Figure 5C).

claim: FcRL5+T-bet+ atypical MBCs positively correlate with anti-erythrocyte IgG antibodies in P. falciparum patients
source: The analysis of memory B-cell subsets and anti-erythrocyte IgG antibodies resembles the anti-PS IgG antibodies correlations, showing a positive significant correlation between FcRL5+T-bet+ atypical MBCs.
evidence: Data from correlation analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2

claim: Plasma cells positively correlate with anti-erythrocyte IgG antibodies in P. falciparum patients
source: A positive correlation was observed with plasma cells, suggesting that other autoantibodies besides anti-PS are produced by these cells, possibly explaining the previous correlation of plasma cells with hemoglobin levels (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).

claim: Anti-DNA antibodies do not correlate with atypical MBCs in P. falciparum patients
source: We did not observe any significant correlation with atypical MBCs, suggesting that anti-DNA antibodies are not predominantly produced by this subpopulation of B-cells.
evidence: Data from correlation analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3

claim: Anti-PfEBA IgG antibodies do not significantly correlate with any B-cell subsets in P. falciparum patients
source: This analysis showed no significant correlation between anti-PfEBA IgG antibodies and any of the B-cells subsets assessed (Figure 6).

claim: FcRL5+T-bet+ B-cells expand robustly when PBMC from healthy donors are incubated with P. falciparum-infected erythrocyte lysates compared to uninfected erythrocyte lysate or no stimulation
source: We observed a robust expansion of FcRL5+T-bet+ B-cells compared to cells incubated with uninfected erythrocyte lysate or with no stimulation (Figure 7A).

claim: FcRL5+ cells enriched from PBMC stimulated with P. falciparum-infected erythrocyte lysate show significantly increased numbers of anti-PS-specific B-cells compared to enriched CD27+ cells
source: Remarkably, ELISPOT analysis of the antibody specificity of enriched FcRL5+ cells showed significantly increased numbers of anti-PS-specific B-cells in the FcRL5+ population when compared to enriched CD27+ cells, which would represent predominantly classical memory B-cells and plasmablast/plasma cells (Figure 7B).

claim: There is no significant difference between the number of FcRL5+ antibody-secreting cells producing anti-PS and the number producing anti-PfEBA
source: No significant difference is observed between the number of FcRL5+antibody-secreting cells (ASCs) producing anti-PS and the number of anti-PfEBA cells

claim: CD27+-enriched cells have higher numbers of total antibody-secreting cells than FcRL5+ cells
source: However, we observed that CD27+-enriched cells had higher numbers of total ASCs than FcLR5+ (Figure 7—figure supplement 1)

claim: Stimulation of PBMC with P. falciparum HRPII does not induce significant expansion of FcRL5+T-bet+ cells
source: Stimulation of PBMC with a specific P. falciparum antigen, Histidine Rich Protein II (HRPII), or with uninfected erythrocyte lysate did not induce a significant expansion of FcRL5+T-bet+ cells in these cultures (Figure 7—figure supplement 2).

claim: Stimulation of PBMC with uninfected erythrocyte lysate does not induce significant expansion of FcRL5+T-bet+ cells
source: Stimulation of PBMC with a specific P. falciparum antigen, Histidine Rich Protein II (HRPII), or with uninfected erythrocyte lysate did not induce a significant expansion of FcRL5+T-bet+ cells in these cultures (Figure 7—figure supplement 2).

claim: Optimal expansion of FcRL5+T-bet+ cells in vitro requires B-cell receptor stimulation, specific inflammatory cytokines (IFNγ/IL-21), and Plasmodium DNA
source: This may be explained by the observation that the three different signals that are needed for optimal expansion of these cells in vitro—B-cell receptor stimulation, specific inflammatory cytokines (IFNγ/ ΙL−21) and Plasmodium DNA (Phalke and Marrack, 2018; Rivera-Correa et al., 2017)—are present in the co-cultures of PBMC with infected lysates, but not in co-cultures with uninfected lysates or purified proteins that lack Plasmodium DNA.
evidence: Cited from Phalke and Marrack, 2018 and Rivera-Correa et al., 2017

claim: Atypical FcRL5+T-bet+ B-cells produce anti-PS antibodies upon stimulation with parasite lysates in vitro
source: Taken together, these results indicate that atypical FcRL5+T-bet+ B-cells produce anti-PS antibodies upon stimulation with parasite lysates in vitro
evidence: Data from in vitro experiments shown in Figure 7

claim: Atypical memory B-cells and anti-PS autoantibodies play a crucial role in human malarial anemia
source: These data define a crucial role for atypical memory B-cells and anti-PS autoantibodies in human malarial anemia.
evidence: Summary of findings from the study

claim: T-bet+ B-cells have been widely studied in the context of autoimmunity
source: T-bet+ B-cells have been widely studied in the context of autoimmunity (Myles et al., 2017; Rubtsova et al., 2015; Rubtsova et al., 2013), in particular in relation to systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) (Phalke and Marrack, 2018).
evidence: Cited from Myles et al., 2017; Rubtsova et al., 2015; Rubtsova et al., 2013; Phalke and Marrack, 2018

claim: T-bet+ B-cells have been suggested as major candidates for drivers of the pathological anti-nuclear antibody response in SLE
source: In this context, these cells have been suggested as major candidates for drivers of the pathological anti-nuclear antibody response that mediates the SLE-associated pathologies (Rubtsova et al., 2017; Wang et al., 2018).
evidence: Cited from Rubtsova et al., 2017 and Wang et al., 2018

claim: T-bet is a key marker of atypical MBCs that are expanded in individuals living in malaria endemic areas
source: In the context of malaria, T-bet was found to be a key marker of atypical MBCs that are expanded in individuals living in malaria endemic areas (Obeng-Adjei et al., 2017; Portugal et al., 2017).
evidence: Cited from Obeng-Adjei et al., 2017 and Portugal et al., 2017

claim: Atypical MBCs have markedly reduced effector function and low antibody secretion capacity ex vivo
source: Some studies characterized ex-vivo atypical MBCs that had markedly reduced effector function and low antibody secretion capacity (Obeng-Adjei et al., 2017; Portugal et al., 2017; Portugal et al., 2015).
evidence: Cited from Obeng-Adjei et al., 2017; Portugal et al., 2017; Portugal et al., 2015

claim: Both atypical and classical MBCs from malaria patients are capable of secreting antibodies against blood-stage P. falciparum antigens
source: Although the unresponsiveness of these cells to direct ex-vivo stimulation with different standard stimuli suggested that these cells were inactive (Obeng-Adjei et al., 2017), both atypical and classical MBCs from malaria patients are capable of secreting antibodies against blood-stage P. falciparum antigens (Krishnamurty et al., 2016; Lugaajju et al., 2017; Muellenbeck et al., 2013; Portugal et al., 2017) (Kim et al., 2019; Pérez-Mazliah et al., 2018; Sundling et al., 2019).
evidence: Cited from multiple sources including Krishnamurty et al., 2016; Lugaajju et al., 2017; Muellenbeck et al., 2013; Portugal et al., 2017; Kim et al., 2019; Pérez-Mazliah et al., 2018; Sundling et al., 2019

claim: Atypical MBCs in Plasmodium-infected mice are short-lived and do not contribute to the long-lived anti-malaria immune response
source: Atypical MBCs have also been described in Plasmodium-infected mice, where they were characterized as short-lived, and therefore not contributing to the long-lived anti malaria immune response (Pérez-Mazliah et al., 2018)

claim: Atypical MBCs in Plasmodium-infected mice limit the protective anti-parasite antibody response
source: Atypical MBCs have also been described in Plasmodium-infected mice, where they were characterized as short-lived, and therefore not contributing to the long-lived anti malaria immune response (Pérez-Mazliah et al., 2018), but where they were able to limit the protective anti-parasite antibody response (Guthmiller et al., 2017).

claim: T-bet+ B-cells are the main producers of anti-PS IgG antibodies during malarial anemia in mice
source: In our previous study in mice, we characterized T-bet+ B-cells as the main producers of anti-PS IgG antibodies during malarial anemia (Rivera-Correa et al., 2017).

claim: The correlation of expansion of atypical MBCs with anemia in patients suggests that these cells have a role in malaria pathogenesis
source: The correlation of expansion of atypical MBCs with anemia in patients suggests that these cells have a role in malaria pathogenesis, providing clinical significance to our findings.
evidence: Inference from correlation data presented in the study

claim: T-bet+ B-cells in mice are activated directly by Plasmodium DNA through TLR-9 alongside IFN-γ to produce anti-PS antibodies
source: T-bet+ B-cells in these mice are activated directly by Plasmodium DNA through TLR-9 alongside IFN-γ to produce anti-PS antibodies (Rivera-Correa et al., 2017).

claim: Atypical T-bet+FcRL5+ memory B-cells contribute to malarial anemia in P. falciparum-infected patients through anti-PS antibody secretion
source: Collectively, results from the analysis of patient samples and from in vitro stimulation of healthy PBMC, suggest that atypical T-bet+FcRL5+ memory B-cells contribute to malarial anemia in P.-falciparum-infected patients through anti-PS antibody secretion.
evidence: Summary of findings from patient samples and in vitro experiments

claim: Atypical T-bet+FcRL5+ B-cells are major promoters of autoimmune-mediated malaria anemia in P. falciparum infections
source: In summary, our results provide the first mechanistic evidence of autoimmune-mediated malaria anemia in patients, and suggest that atypical T-bet+FcRL5+ B-cells are major promoters of this pathology in P.-falciparum-infections.

claim: The study cohort consisted of 24 P. falciparum-infected patients with 31 unique samples
source: In this study, we focused on samples (24 patients, 31 unique samples) from a cohort of P.-falciparum-infected returned travelers from Germany, who acquired malaria while visiting Africa.

claim: The P. falciparum strain 3D7 was used for in vitro culture experiments
source: Erythrocyte asexual stage cultures of the P. falciparum strain 3D7 were maintained at 5% hematocrit in RPMI 1640

claim: Ionomycin treatment at 2.5 µM induces PS exposure in erythrocytes
source: First, fresh healthy donor erythrocytes were treated with ionomycin at 2.5 µM (Life Technologies) to stress erythrocytes and to induce exposure of PS (Lang et al., 2006).

claim: The expression of T-bet is significantly higher in FcRL5+ cells compared to classical MBCs
source: To define the atypical and classical MBC populations better, we analyzed the expression of T-bet in FcRL5+ cells compared to classical MBCs, finding that the expression of T-bet is significantly higher in FcRL5+ cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
